title: Knapsack
summary: Knapsack DP picks items under a budget. Rows add one item at a time and columns are every budget from 0 up, so each cell decides: skip this item, or take it and use the best answer for the budget that is left.
idea: dp[i][c] = best using the first i items within budget c = max(skip: dp[i−1][c], take: dp[i−1][c−w] + v). Reading the same row instead allows unlimited copies.

signals.see: Choose a subset of items with weights or costs, under a capacity, to maximise value or hit an exact total.
signals.think: That is 0/1 knapsack. The state is (items considered, capacity used).

signals.see: 'Can the numbers be split into two equal halves?', 'Is there a subset with sum k?'
signals.think: Subset sum is knapsack with true or false cells: can[s] |= can[s − x].

signals.see: Coins or pieces can be reused any number of times.
signals.think: Unbounded knapsack: take reads the same row (dp[c − w]), so the item can be used again.

phrasings: Pack a bag of limited weight to carry the most value.
Can a list of numbers be split into two groups with the same sum?
Find the fewest coins that make an amount, with unlimited coins of each kind.

picture.title: Every subset versus an item × capacity table
picture.alt: On the left, every subset of items is tried, which is 2 to the n options. On the right, a table has a row per item and a column per capacity; each cell takes the larger of skipping the item (the cell above) and taking it (the cell above and w columns left, plus its value).
picture.caption: Skip copies the cell above; take reads w columns to the left in the row above.

visualiser.inputHelp: Up to 4 weights from 1 to 6, one value from 1 to 30 for each, and a capacity from 1 to 6.

oneLiner: for item (w, v): for c from cap down to w: best[c] = max(best[c], best[c-w] + v)

exercise.prompt: Return true if the numbers can be split into two groups with equal sums. Every number goes into exactly one group. Use one boolean array where can[s] says some of the numbers seen so far add up to s. The starter loops s upwards, so it can reuse a number twice.
hints: If the total is odd, the answer is false. Otherwise look for a subset that sums to half the total.
can[0] is true. For each number x, can[s] becomes true if can[s − x] was already true.
Loop s downwards from half to x, so can[s − x] still describes the numbers before x.

complexity.why: There is one cell per item and capacity, each filled in constant time. Looping capacity downwards lets one row stand in for the whole table. This is pseudo-polynomial: it depends on the capacity's size.

mistakes: Looping capacity upwards in the one-row 0/1 version, which lets an item be taken twice.
Looping downwards for unbounded problems, which forbids reusing an item.
Using 0 instead of 'impossible' (infinity or false) for amounts that cannot be made exactly.
Forgetting the odd-total check when splitting into equal halves.

quiz.question: In the one-row 0/1 knapsack, why loop capacity from high to low?
choices: So best[c − w] still holds the value from before this item, and each item is used at most once
quiz.explain: Going upwards would read a cell already updated with this item.

quiz.question: How does unbounded knapsack (unlimited copies) differ?
choices: Take reads the current row, so loop capacity upwards
It cannot be solved with DP
quiz.explain: Reading the updated cell means the item can be taken again.

quiz.question: Is O(n × capacity) polynomial in the input size?
choices: No: it is pseudo-polynomial, because capacity can be huge compared with its number of digits
quiz.explain: A capacity of a billion makes the table huge, even though it is one number.

interviewTip: Draw the item × capacity table for a tiny case first. Then show the one-row version and explain the loop direction; that is the usual follow-up.
